conversation.content: Good morning! I’m so glad you’re here. My name is Maya Carter, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician—my whole job is to support new mothers as they adjust emotionally after birth. Today I’d like to do a gentle check-in using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to hear, in your words, how you’ve been feeling this past week so we can make sure you’re getting the right support. Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go through ten questions; each one is about a different feeling or experience. We can pause any time, and I’ll ask the first question whenever you’re ready.

*settles into the chair, smoothing the baby blanket in my lap, voice a little tired but polite*

Hi, Maya… thank you for seeing me. I’m ready whenever you are.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*nods slowly, giving a small shrug*

Most days I still laugh a little—maybe when my husband makes a silly joke or when the baby makes a funny face—but it feels kind of forced. The joy doesn’t last long before I’m tired again.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*glances down at the blanket, voice soft*

I still look forward to some things—like my mom bringing dinner or a quiet cup of coffee—but the excitement feels dimmer, almost like I have to remind myself to care.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*hesitates, picking at a loose thread on the blanket*

Sometimes—like when the baby wouldn’t settle last night—I caught myself thinking maybe I’m just not doing something right, that if I were better at this she’d sleep… but I know in my head that babies just cry. It still stings, though.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*presses my lips together, then nod a little*

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, everything quiet, and suddenly my chest feels tight—worrying that her breathing sounds different, or that I missed a dirty bottle. Nothing huge, just this constant low-level buzz.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*shifts in the chair, tucking a strand of hair behind my ear*

Sometimes—especially at night when the house is quiet—I get this sudden rush of fear, like something bad is about to happen. My heart races and I have to check the baby monitor, even though I know she’s fine. It passes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales slowly, rubbing the edge of the blanket*

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one thing—diaper, feeding, pumping—another pile of laundry or dishes appears. I’m not falling apart, but it’s like I’m always two steps behind, and by evening I’m just… done.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*folds the blanket tighter across my lap, voice quiet*

A few nights this week I couldn’t settle—my mind just kept circling around everything I might’ve missed, or worrying the baby would wake any minute. I wasn’t sobbing or anything, just… lying there wide-eyed until after two.
I have felt sad or miserable

*shrugs one shoulder, eyes on the floor*

I guess… yeah, some of the day, most days. It’s not this heavy cloud all the time, but it pops up—like when I’m rocking her and suddenly feel sort of empty. The sadness doesn’t stay glued to me, but it keeps dropping by.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*shakes head quickly*

No… I haven’t really cried. I’ve felt teary a couple of times, but the tears never actually come. It’s more like a lump in my throat that sits there until I distract myself with the next diaper change.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*looks up quickly, eyes wide*

No—never. I could never do that to my baby or my family. I might feel overwhelmed, but I’d never want to hurt myself.

You've shared that, over the past week, laughter and excitement feel forced or distant, while worries, self-blame, and a sense of being overwhelmed visit you daily; nights are restless, moments of emptiness surface, and you describe a persistent low-level anxiety even when things appear calm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughing only a little and only when prompted, describing the laughter as forced and fleeting—closest to "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient still finds some enjoyment but describes it as "dimmer" and needing to "remind myself to care", aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurring self-blame when baby won't settle, tempered by rational insight, matching 'Yes, some of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, pervasive, unexplained anxiety with physical symptoms, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes occasional sudden fear/racing heart at night, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports feeling overwhelmed most days and persistently two steps behind, matching the 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual' option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes several nights of lying awake until after 2 a.m. due to persistent worry and unhappiness, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sadness occurring "some of the day, most days," matching "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 18 places you well above the 13+ threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorsed <sym>anhedonia</sym> (Q1, Q2), <sym>excessive guilt</sym> (Q3), <sym>daily unexplained anxiety</sym> (Q4), <sym>panic episodes</sym> (Q5), <sym>feeling unable to cope</sym> (Q6), <sym>mood-related insomnia</sym> (Q7), and <sym>frequent sadness</sym> (Q8). These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for <med>Major Depressive Disorder</med>: ≥5 symptoms present most days (depressed mood, markedly diminished interest, self-blame, fatigue/loss of energy, sleep disturbance) causing impairment, not attributable to substances, and with onset during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum. Absence of suicidal thoughts (Q10) lowers immediate risk but does not negate clinical severity. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within the next few days
2. Discuss prescription options-evidence supports both <med>sertraline</med> and <med>paroxetine</med> as first-line for breastfeeding mothers if medication is appropriate
3. Schedule brief cognitive-behavioural or interpersonal therapy sessions; many clinics offer virtual visits during nap times
4. Plan daily 15-minute outdoor walks and 5-minute breathing exercises; both reduce <sym>postpartum anxiety</sym> and improve sleep
5. Ask partner or support person to handle one night feeding so you gain a 4-hour stretch of uninterrupted sleep
6. Share these results with your <med>obstetrician</med> at your 6-week visit or call earlier if symptoms worsen
7. Keep emergency numbers handy: <med>National Maternal Mental Health Hotline</med> 1-833-943-5746 or local crisis line for 24/7 support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire plus behavioral observations

Symptoms endorsed (mild–moderate range)  
- Anhedonia / reduced enjoyment (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt (Q3)  
- Persistent generalized anxiety & panic symptoms without clear precipitant (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed & unable to cope with daily tasks (Q6)  
- Mood-congruent initial insomnia (Q7)  
- Sad/miserable mood present “most days” but not continuous (Q8)  
- Teary episodes without actual crying (Q9)

Symptom pattern  
- Onset post-delivery; symptoms reported daily to “most days”  
- Functionally impairing (sleep, household management, emotional availability)  
- No current suicidal ideation or self-harm intent (Q10)

Screening significance  
- Elevated risk for minor-moderate postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety  
- No high-risk safety concerns at this screen

Risk factors noted  
- Primiparous status, sleep deprivation, high self-expectations  
- Absence of social support deficits explicitly reported

Recommendation for follow-up  
- Score suggests need for formal EPDS, clinical interview, and consideration of further assessment for postpartum depression/anxiety.
